primary_summary: This video explains how to correctly perform the frog pose, a popular hip mobility stretch. It highlights common errors, such as compensating with spinal movement and losing proper knee/ankle contact, and provides a detailed biomechanical explanation along with a corrected technique to ensure genuine hip joint mobility.

classification.usefulness_reason: The video provides a clear biomechanical explanation of a common hip mobility exercise, identifies frequent errors and compensation patterns, and offers a detailed, corrected technique with specific cues for proper execution. This is valuable for diagnostic support, explanation support, corrective exercise selection, and biomechanical concept retrieval.

problem_statements: Incorrect frog pose technique leading to compensation
Chasing stretch sensation over genuine hip joint movement
Compensating with low back/spine during hip abduction stretches
Losing proper inner knee and inner ankle contact during frog pose
Creating more tension when stretching too hard
habits_or_contexts: Performing frog pose for hip mobility
key_visual_points: Animated skeleton showing hip external rotation and abduction in frog pose.

advice_mentioned: Focus on genuine hip movement rather than just a maximal stretch sensation.
Maintain contact with the inside of the knee and the very front side of the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus).
Keep the spine neutral during the stretch.
Gently separate shoulder blades away from the spine.
Stop moving hips back when contacts are lost, jamming is felt in the hips, or spinal movement occurs.
warnings_or_limitations: Forcing a stretch can create more tension, which is counterproductive for relaxation.
Losing proper knee and ankle contacts can lead to compensatory spinal movement or jamming in the hip joint.

knowledge_units.title: Common Errors and Compensations in Frog Pose
knowledge_units.summary: Many individuals perform the frog pose incorrectly by prioritizing a maximal stretch sensation, which often leads to compensatory movement from the spine and low back instead of genuine hip joint mobility. This incorrect technique typically involves rolling onto the middle of the knee and losing crucial contact with the inner knee and inner ankle.
observable_signs: Rolling onto the middle of the knee
Loss of contact with the inside of the knee
Loss of contact with the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus)
Excessive arching or movement in the low back/spine
Feeling a 'bigger stretch' in the groin that may not be indicative of genuine hip mobility
mechanisms: Insufficient genuine hip abduction and external rotation range of motion.
Attempting to achieve a deeper stretch by compensating with movement from the lumbar spine.
Altered joint mechanics at the knee and ankle due to improper weight distribution and contact points.
errors_to_avoid: Forcing a deep stretch beyond genuine hip range of motion.
Losing contact with the inner knee or inner ankle.
Allowing the spine to arch or move excessively to compensate for hip immobility.

knowledge_units.title: Optimized Frog Pose for Genuine Hip Mobility
knowledge_units.summary: To effectively stretch the hip adductors and improve hip external rotation and abduction, focus on maintaining specific contact points and controlled movement. This ensures genuine movement within the hip joint, preventing spinal compensation and maximizing mobility gains.
mechanisms: Maintaining specific ground contacts (inner knee, inner ankle) ensures the femur moves genuinely within the hip socket (acetabulum).
Neutral spine position isolates hip movement and prevents compensatory lumbar extension.
Gentle, controlled movement promotes active range of motion and reduces passive overstretching.
execution_steps: Start in a quadruped position (on hands and knees).
Widen the knees to a comfortable frog-like stance.
Ensure the inside of the knee maintains contact with the ground.
Ensure the very front side of the inner ankle bone (medial malleolus) maintains contact with the ground.
Adjust your stance (knee width, foot position) until these two contact points are gently established.
Keep your spine in a neutral position, avoiding excessive arching or rounding.
Gently separate your shoulder blades away from your spine.
Slowly and gently set your hips back towards your heels.

Stop the movement at the point just before you feel like you lose any of the established knee or ankle contacts, or if you feel jamming in the front of your hips, or if your spine has to move to any significant extent.
cues: "Find that inside knee and just the very front side of the inner ankle bone."
"Very gently separating your shoulder blades away from your spine."
errors_to_avoid: Losing contact with the inner knee or inner ankle.
Forcing movement beyond the genuine hip range.
Allowing the low back to arch or move excessively.
Feeling jamming or pinching in the front of the hips.
when_useful: To improve hip abduction and external rotation mobility.
To effectively stretch the inner thighs and groin muscles.
To re-educate movement patterns and prevent spinal compensation during hip stretches.
advice: Play around with your stance to find the optimal position for maintaining contacts.
Focus on a mild, genuine stretch rather than a maximal, forced sensation.
